case_studies.title: Agents That Certify Their Own Exploits: Confidence-Scheduled Restricted Responses for Safe Opponent Exploitation
case_studies.abstract: An agent playing a Nash-equilibrium strategy in a two-player zero-sum imperfect-information game secures the game value but forfeits the additional value offered by a flawed opponent. Diffuse deviations pose a particular challenge: binary release rules may gather too little evidence to act, while a full best response to an incomplete opponent model can be highly exploitable. We introduce \emph{budget-constrained confidence-scheduled restricted responses} (CS-RNR), the first opponent-exploitation method whose safety guarantee is a certificate the agent computes on the strategy it actually deplo
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of safely exploiting flawed opponents in two-player games by introducing a new method called budget-constrained confidence-scheduled restricted responses. The authors built a certification system that allows an agent to compute its own safety guarantee. The result is a more reliable way to exploit opponents without risking the game value.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: High novelty and IT relevance, but low 90-day value due to abstract and theoretical nature

case_studies.title: PAUSE: A User-Centric Benchmark for Personal AI Assistants in Unified Service Environments
case_studies.abstract: Personal AI assistants are increasingly deployed as task-oriented, tool-augmented agents that operate within unified service environments to support everyday user activities. In realistic settings, such assistants must reason over persistent user state, respect user-specific configurations and permissions, and sustain long-horizon, constraint-aware interactions across multiple services. Existing benchmarks, however, often fragment service contexts or abstract away user state, limiting their ability to evaluate user-centric personal assistant behavior in realistic service settings. We introduce
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating personal AI assistants in realistic unified service environments. The authors built a benchmark called PAUSE to assess user-centric personal assistant behavior. The result is a more accurate way to evaluate AI assistants, but it's not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on evaluating AI assistant performance rather than managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty score is moderate due to the introduction of a new benchmark. Relevance score is moderate because it discusses unified service environments, which is relevant to the systems IT engineers manage. Value score is moderate because the paper suggests a new approach for evaluating personal AI assistants, but it's unclear if this can be applied to real-world infrastructure in 90 days.

case_studies.title: Stop Shipping AI Agents on Faith: Capability Is Not Production Readiness
case_studies.abstract: AI agents are moving into production workflows where they retrieve information, call tools, maintain state, and act on behalf of users or organizations, but many release decisions still rely on capability signals, demos, or behavioral tests that do not show whether an agent is ready to operate under production constraints. Capability is therefore not production readiness. This paper introduces the ProofAgent Index (PAI), a governance readiness index for AI agents. PAI combines four dimensions of deployment evidence: Evaluation, Context, Compliance, and Governance. Evaluation measures observed
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of determining if AI agents are ready for production by introducing the ProofAgent Index (PAI), a governance readiness index that evaluates an agent's deployment readiness. The authors built the PAI, which combines four dimensions of deployment evidence, and found that capability is not the same as production readiness. The result is a more reliable way to assess whether an AI agent is ready for production use.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI agent deployments, here is what to do: assess your current agents using the four dimensions of the PAI - Evaluation, Context, Compliance, and Governance. Check if your agents meet the production readiness criteria to avoid potential issues. This is directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, especially for those responsible for deploying and managing AI agents in production environments.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty and IT relevance are moderately high because PAI could improve the quality of AI agents in IT environments, while Value_90_days is low since actual implementation of PAI requires more specific guidance.

case_studies.title: Would You Walk to the Car Wash? Revealing the Salience Bias of Large Language Models in Commonsense Reasoning
case_studies.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to advance in complex reasoning tasks, they have learned to heavily prioritize explicit conditions provided in the input. However, in everyday commonsense reasoning, this mechanism exposes a critical vulnerability which we term Salience Bias: models become easily hijacked by useless explicit distractors (e.g., numerical values), leading them to ignore the implicit physical or commonsense prerequisites of a task. A critical open question is whether this failure reflects a genuine gap in commonsense knowledge or merely its suppression under misleading tas
case_studies.summary: Researchers found that large language models can be misled by irrelevant information, causing them to ignore common sense and make incorrect decisions. They built tests to reveal this 'Salience Bias' and showed how it can lead to poor reasoning. This research is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on the limitations of language models in reasoning tasks, rather than cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.score_reasoning: While this research touches on large language models, it's more relevant to NLP academics and ML researchers than IT infrastructure or IT work. It presents some novel insights but its implications for IT and SRE are secondary. IT professionals might use some parts of this research to train or fine-tune their LLMs, but there aren't enough actionable takeaways for this work to score higher for real-world impact within 90 days.

case_studies.title: CoGate: Confidence-Gated Co-Decoding for Secure Code Generation
case_studies.abstract: Large language models are widely used for code generation, but they can also produce insecure programs due to patterns learned from their pretraining data. Decoding-time steering has become an important solution to this problem: a small expert model is combined with the target model at each step to generate more secure code, which is referred to as co-decoding. However, the acceptance rule for existing co-decoding approaches does not consider the expert model's confidence. When the security expert is unconfident due to unseen patterns or out-of-distribution (OOD) contexts, its guidance can the
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of large language models generating insecure code by introducing a confidence-gated co-decoding approach, which builds on existing co-decoding methods by considering the expert model's confidence, resulting in more secure code generation. The researchers built a system called CoGate, which combines a target model with a small expert model at each step to generate secure code. This approach improves the security of code generated by large language models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that uses large language models for code generation, here is what to do: review your current co-decoding approach, consider implementing CoGate or a similar confidence-gated co-decoding method, and evaluate its impact on the security of your generated code. This flags a risk: if your org uses co-decoding for secure code generation, check your expert model's confidence levels immediately. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to those using large language models for code generation.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty is high because the paper introduces a confidence-gated co-decoding approach, which is a new method for secure code generation. However, IT relevance is somewhat low because it's focused on the specific problem of secure code generation, which is not directly relevant to general IT infrastructure, SaaS tooling, or endpoint management. Value in 90 days is low because it's not clear how quickly an IT engineer or consultant can adapt this method to their workflow or propose it as a service to a client.

case_studies.title: Correcting Mode Collapse in Silicon Sampling with Semantic Similarity Rating
case_studies.abstract: Silicon sampling refers to the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate responses to surveys. It has shown promise, but tends to generate response distributions with unrealistically low variance. We argue that this mode collapse is due to LLMs failure to generate numeric data, and that text responses may be better suited for this task. We analyze whether Semantic Similarity Rating can improve the fidelity of silicon sampling responses when asked about political attitudes. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of mode collapse in silicon sampling, a method that uses Large Language Models to generate survey responses, by using Semantic Similarity Rating to improve response fidelity. The authors built a system that maps text responses to a numeric scale using text embeddings. The result shows improved fidelity of silicon sampling responses when asked about political attitudes.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on improving survey response generation using Large Language Models.

case_studies.title: AI systems and the reproduction of (standard) language ideologies in World Englishes
case_studies.abstract: The rapid growth of large language models (LLMs) has resurrected age-old questions in sociolinguistics and world Englishes, such as who decides what counts as legitimate English, whose English is suspect etc. This paper examines how AI systems, their uses and discourse on them reflect, reinforce, and occasionally challenge (standard) language ideologies, which privilege Inner Circle norms and marginalize non-dominant Englishes. case_studies.summary: This research explores how AI systems reflect and reinforce standard language ideologies, potentially marginalizing non-dominant Englishes. It examines the impact of AI on language norms and challenges. The result highlights the need for diversity in language models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: Pure academic novelty with no IT angle, moderate novelty within the AI field, but low value 90 days, high IT_relevance_score would've bumped total score higher, but IT_relevance score is only 2.

case_studies.title: StealthBench: Measuring Operational Stealth in Autonomous Offensive-Security Agents
case_studies.abstract: Stealth, the discipline of achieving an objective without revealing your presence, capabilities, or collected intelligence, is what separates sophisticated operators from detectable ones. Elite security researchers and advanced persistent threats achieve their objectives unnoticed; autonomous agents increasingly inherit the same offensive tasks, but do they inherit the tradecraft? We introduce StealthBench,a benchmark that measures operational stealth in autonomous offensive-security agents across six operational security (OPSEC) dimensions. We extract 11 hand-verified OPSEC incidents from rea
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of measuring the stealth capabilities of autonomous offensive-security agents, introducing a benchmark called StealthBench that evaluates these agents across six operational security dimensions, resulting in a better understanding of their ability to operate undetected. The StealthBench benchmark can help identify areas where autonomous agents may reveal their presence or capabilities. This can inform the development of more sophisticated autonomous security agents.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage autonomous security agents, here is what to do: review the StealthBench benchmark, assess your agents' performance across the six OPSEC dimensions, and adjust their configuration to improve their stealth capabilities. This flags a risk: if your org uses autonomous security agents, check their OPSEC incident history immediately to identify potential vulnerabilities. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to security teams managing autonomous agents.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novel benchmark for autonomous security agents, relevant to IT security professionals, but unclear practical value within 90 days.

case_studies.title: TraceCoder: Explainable and Auditable Code Generation with Position-Key Snippet Versioning
case_studies.abstract: Contemporary LLM-based coding agents produce code as black-box outputs: the rationale behind each line is hidden, the evolution of the code through benchmark-driven repair is ephemeral, and post-hoc auditing is impossible. We present a code generation concept that addresses these shortcomings through three complementary mechanisms: (i) a relational snippet-history schema that records, per repair event, the benchmark reference, round number, failure text, and LLM explanation, enabling full provenance queries; (ii) a browser-based visualisation tool that renders this history as heat-mapped, hove
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of explainable code generation by creating a system called TraceCoder, which provides a transparent and auditable way of generating code. The system uses a relational snippet-history schema and a visualisation tool to record and display the evolution of code. The result is a more trustworthy and understandable code generation process.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI-powered code generation tools, here is what to do: review your current tools for explainability and auditing capabilities, consider integrating TraceCoder or similar systems to improve transparency, and assess the potential impact on your code development workflow.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a novel concept, TraceCoder, for explainable and auditable code generation. It addresses a significant issue with black-box LLM-based coding agents, which is highly relevant to the IT community. However, the practical application and automation potential within 90 days are limited.
